newsitem.title: GERMANY: Party is over for German bank shares, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Party is over for German bank shares, analysts say.

text.p: German banking shares, among the stock market's top performers this year, have run out of steam because investors are likely to be deterred by a slowdown in earnings growth in 1997, analysts said on Thursday.
But they said takeover speculation would continue to underpin the share prices and cause sporadic surges in selected stocks.

"It is increasingly difficult to make a case for pursuing them any further," said Bryan Crossley, banking analyst at ABN Amro Hoare Govett in London. "I would be amazed if banks maintain their earnings growth this year."
"Although comments on the first two months have been universally upbeat they don't require much of an upward revision of existing projections for 1997 and 1998.
"On that basis the evaluation of most of these banks seems rather stretched."
The shares of top listed banks fell on Thursday as the market's focus shifted to carmakers, whose exports are set to benefit from the recent weakening of the mark, traders said.

The top four banks reported operating profit gains of between 18.4 and 43.8 percent in 1996, buoyed by big increases in commission income and, in most cases, by strong earnings from the sale of bonds held in their liquidity portfolios.
Analysts said banks were unlikely to keep up that growth in 1997 given mounting concern that this year's rally in world share and bond markets might have been excessive and could be reversed.

Dieter Hein, banking analyst at BHF-Bank in Frankfurt, predicted banks would achieve operating profit growth of between 10 and 20 percent this year and said his overall weighting for the German banking sector was neutral.

The top three banks, Deutsche Bank AG, Dresdner Bank AG and Commerzbank AG, have all outperformed the DAX index of 30 blue chip stocks this year. They made respective gains of 25 percent, 28 percent and 19 percent up to Thursday against a 17.6 percent rise in the DAX.

Bavarian banks Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel- Bank AG (Hypo-Bank), most often cited as candidates for potential takeover or merger, have chalked up gains of six percent and 17 percent.

Those two stocks soared in the second half of last year after Deutsche said in July it had amassed a 5.21 percent stake in Vereinsbank -- a move that unleashed takeover speculation in a market regarded as heavily overbanked and in need of consolidation.

Hypo-Bank, Germany's fifth-largest listed bank, in particular has been the subject of takeover rumours in recent weeks with speculation focusing on a possible link-up with Dresdner or with local rival Vereinsbank.
Top bankers have sought to quell the speculation, saying any takeover would be prohibitively expensive.
Dresdner chief executive Juergen Sarrazin said on Thursday that hostile banking takeovers were not an "acute" issue but added that his bank would not play a passive role if merger activity broke out.
Hein at BHF-Bank issued a sell recommendation on shares in Hypo-Bank, saying the bank needed to raise capital because its Tier I capital ratio declined last year to 4.5 percent from 5.1 percent.
Hypo-Bank was alone in sustaining an 8.7 percent fall in operating profit last year, due to a 58 percent surge in risk provisions which Hein said pointed to concealed risks in its loan portfolio.
Hein's favourite is Vereinsbank, which he said will not need a capital raising soon and which showed solid profit growth last year.
Crossley at ABN Amro Hoare Govett has a buy recommendation for Commerzbank given the substantial improvement in underlying profitability in the last three years.
He has a sell recommendation on Deutsche, partly because of the bank's strong cost growth, but regards Dresdner, Hypo-Bank and Vereinsbank as "holds".
